title: Transactions and Isolation
summary: Group changes into InnoDB transactions with START TRANSACTION, COMMIT, ROLLBACK and SAVEPOINT, understand autocommit and implicit commits, choose an isolation level and handle lock waits and.
introduction: Selling two bags of coffee means lowering the stock and inserting an order; if the server crashes between those statements, the shop has sold coffee it still thinks it has. A transaction makes several statements succeed or fail as one unit. InnoDB gives every MySQL table that guarantee, but only if you know when a transaction starts, which statements commit it without asking, and how concurrent transactions see each other's changes. This lesson covers all three.
learningObjectives: Start, commit and roll back transactions and use savepoints
Explain autocommit and the statements that commit implicitly
Describe the four isolation levels and InnoDB's REPEATABLE READ default
Lock rows with SELECT ... FOR UPDATE and react to deadlocks

blocks.text: By default every statement is its own transaction: MySQL commits it the moment it finishes, which is what `@@autocommit = 1` means. `START TRANSACTION` (or `BEGIN`) suspends that until you say `COMMIT` or `ROLLBACK`. The second variable below is the isolation level, explained further down.

`SET autocommit = 0` makes every statement in the session part of an open transaction until you commit. It is easy to forget the `COMMIT` and hold locks for hours, so explicit `START TRANSACTION` blocks are the safer habit.
Inside a transaction your own session sees its changes immediately; other sessions keep seeing the old rows until you commit. `ROLLBACK` throws the changes away as if they had never happened.

blocks.text: A savepoint marks a position inside a transaction. `ROLLBACK TO` undoes everything after the mark but keeps the transaction open, which lets an application retry one step without redoing the whole unit. The final `ROLLBACK` here discards the price change as well, so the data is unchanged afterwards.

blocks.text: A real transaction: selling two bags

A sale is two writes that must both happen. `SELECT ... FOR UPDATE` locks the stock row until the transaction ends, so a second checkout for the same coffee waits instead of both reading 40 and both succeeding. The application checks that the stock is sufficient, then updates and inserts, and commits only when every step worked.

blocks.text: `COMMIT` makes both changes durable at once: Hannah has her first order (id 8) and Morning Blend is at 38. Had the `INSERT` failed, for instance on a foreign key, the application would issue `ROLLBACK` and the stock would be untouched. The `UNSIGNED` stock column is a second safety net: subtracting below zero fails with error 1690 under strict mode instead of wrapping around.

blocks.title: Schema statements commit for you
blocks.text: `CREATE TABLE`, `ALTER TABLE`, `DROP`, `TRUNCATE`, `CREATE INDEX`, `CREATE USER` and `GRANT` cause an *implicit commit* before they run and cannot be rolled back. A migration that mixes a data fix with an `ALTER TABLE` therefore commits the fix early, and a `ROLLBACK` afterwards does nothing. Keep schema changes and data changes in separate transactions, and check with `SHOW TABLE STATUS` that your tables really are InnoDB: the legacy MyISAM engine ignores transactions without a word.
Isolation decides what a transaction sees of changes that other transactions make at the same time. Higher levels prevent more anomalies and take more locks.

rows: sees uncommitted changes of others; avoid
each statement sees what was committed when it started; PostgreSQL's default
InnoDB's default; consistent snapshot from the first read, so plain reads also avoid phantoms
plain SELECTs lock the rows they read; safest and slowest

blocks.text: Under `REPEATABLE READ`, each transaction reads from a snapshot taken at its first `SELECT`, so repeated reads return the same rows even while other sessions commit. The walkthrough below needs two client windows:

rows: `START TRANSACTION;` then `SELECT stock FROM coffees WHERE id = 1;` returns 38
`UPDATE coffees SET stock = 50 WHERE id = 1;` commits at once (autocommit)
`SELECT stock FROM coffees WHERE id = 1;` still returns 38, from the snapshot

blocks.text: Locking reads (`FOR UPDATE`, `UPDATE`, `DELETE`) always work on the latest committed data and take row locks, which is why the sale above used one. `SET SESSION TRANSACTION ISOLATION LEVEL READ COMMITTED;` switches a session to the level PostgreSQL uses, where each statement sees what was committed when it started; it is a common choice for write-heavy workloads because InnoDB takes fewer gap locks there.

A transaction that needs a row another transaction has locked waits up to `innodb_lock_wait_timeout` seconds (50 by default) and then fails. When two transactions each wait for the other, InnoDB detects the deadlock immediately, rolls back the one that did less work and reports it. Both errors are normal in a busy system; the application must catch them and retry the whole transaction.

blocks.code:
-- Session B, while session A holds the lock on coffee 1
SELECT stock FROM coffees WHERE id = 1 FOR UPDATE;

blocks.content: ERROR 1205 (HY000): Lock wait timeout exceeded; try restarting transaction

blocks.text: The deadlock message is `ERROR 1213 (40001): Deadlock found when trying to get lock; try restarting transaction`, and `SHOW ENGINE INNODB STATUS\G` prints the latest one in detail. Prevent most deadlocks by keeping transactions short, touching rows in a consistent order (always coffees before orders, for example) and committing promptly.

blocks.title: Transactions in application code
blocks.text: Drivers expose the same statements: `beginTransaction()`, `commit()` and `rollback()` on a connection in Node's mysql2, or `connection.commit()` in Python's connectors. A transaction belongs to one connection, so never spread its statements across a connection pool, and always release the connection after `COMMIT` or `ROLLBACK`.

questions.question: An `ALTER TABLE` inside a transaction can be undone with ROLLBACK.
questions.explanation: Schema statements cause an implicit commit before they run and cannot be rolled back. Keep them out of data transactions.

questions.question: What should an application do after receiving error 1213 (deadlock)?
questions.explanation: InnoDB has already rolled back the losing transaction. The correct response is to retry the whole transaction from the start, usually after a short pause.
options: Run COMMIT to keep the partial work
